steps.text:
NVIDIA MIG (Multi‑Instance GPU) is a hardware‑level feature introduced with the NVIDIA A100 (and later GPUs) that lets a single physical GPU be partitioned into multiple isolated “instances,” each with its own dedicated compute, memory, and cache resources. ### Key points | Aspect | Details | |--------|---------| | **Purpose** | Increase GPU utilization and flexibility by allowing different workloads (or users) to share a single GPU without interfering with each other. | | **How it works** | The GPU’s resources (SMs, memory, memory bandwidth, caches, etc.) are sliced into up to 7 (​A100) or more instances. Each instance appears to the system as an independent logical GPU. | | **Isolation** | Each MIG instance has its own driver context, memory address space, and hardware queues, providing strong security and performance isolation. | | **Supported workloads** | Ideal for inference serving, batch processing, and any scenario where many smaller jobs can run in parallel (e.g., multiple containers, VMs, or Kubernetes pods). | | **Software integration** | Exposed through NVIDIA CUDA, NVIDIA Container Toolkit, and Kubernetes device plugins. You can request a specific MIG profile (e.g., 1 GPU → 2 × “1g.5gb” instances). | | **Management** | MIG can be configured via `nvidia-smi` (`--mig-mode`, `--create-gpu-instance`, `--create-compute-instance`) or via orchestration tools that automate profile creation. | | **Benefits** | • Higher overall GPU utilization
• Better workload isolation and security
• Ability to run many small jobs on a single GPU
• Simplifies multi‑tenant environments (e.g., shared clusters). | | **Limitations** | • Not all GPU models support MIG (primarily A100, A30, and newer Ampere/Hopper GPUs).
• The number and size of instances are fixed once created; you must delete/re‑create to change them.
• Certain features (e.g., GPU‑direct RDMA) may have restrictions within MIG. | In practice, when you enable MIG on a compatible GPU, you decide on a set of **MIG profiles** (combinations of compute units and memory). Each profile becomes a virtual GPU that can be assigned to containers, VMs, or jobs just like a physical GPU, giving you the flexibility to match the size of the GPU instance to the needs of each workload.

**NVIDIA MIG (Multi‑Instance GPU) is only available on a subset of NVIDIA’s data‑center GPUs that expose the required hardware slicing capability.**  

| GPU family (Ampere & Hopper) | Specific models that support MIG | Notes |
|------------------------------|----------------------------------|-------|
| **A100** (PCIe & SXM) | A100 {{int:32:48}} GB, A100 {{int:64:96}} GB, A100 PCIe, A100 SXM4, A100 SXM5 | The flagship MIG‑enabled GPU; can be partitioned into up to 7 instances (or {{int:11:17}} instances on the {{int:64:96}} GB model with “MIG‑v2”). |
| **A30** | A30 PCIe, A30 SXM4 | Supports up to 4 instances (each “1g.5gb”, “2g.10gb”, etc.). |
| **A10** | A10 PCIe, A10 SXM4 | Supports up to 4 instances (smaller profiles than A30). |
| **H100** (Hopper) | H100 PCIe, H100 SXM5 | MIG is carried forward and can be split into up to 8 instances (or {{int:11:17}} instances with the newer “MIG‑v2” mode). |
| **A40** (and other RTX/GeForce cards) | **No** – MIG is *not* enabled on consumer‑grade RTX/GeForce GPUs (e.g., RTX {{int:2464:3696}}, RTX {{int:2472:3708}}). | Those cards lack the hardware slicing block required for MIG. |
| **Other older data‑center GPUs** (e.g., V100, T4, P100) | **No** – MIG was introduced with the Ampere architecture. | You can still use Multi‑Process Service (MPS) for sharing, but not MIG. |

### Quick checklist for a given GPU
1. **Architecture** – Must be **Ampere** (GA100/GA10x) or **Hopper** (GH100).  
2. **SKU** – Only the data‑center SKUs listed above expose MIG; the same silicon in a “RTX/GeForce” SKU does not.  
3. **Driver / CUDA version** – MIG support starts with NVIDIA driver {{int:368:552}}.x (for A100) and newer, and CUDA 11.0+ (or later). Keep the driver up‑to‑date to enable the MIG‑mode commands (`nvidia-smi --mig-mode`).  

If you’re planning to provision a cluster or a VM pool that will use MIG, make sure the host machines are equipped with one of the GPUs in the table and that the appropriate driver version is installed. Once the GPU is in **MIG‑mode**, you can create GPU‑instances and compute‑instances via `nvidia-smi` or through orchestration tools (Kubernetes device plugin, NVIDIA Container Toolkit, etc.).
